title: Credit controls and the silver crash knock shares down 10 percent
what: On 14 March President Carter announced the first credit controls since the Second World War, with limits on lending, credit cards and instalment loans, as inflation and short-term interest rates both stood near 18 percent. On 27 March the silver market collapsed: silver fell to 10.80 dollars an ounce from over 50 in January after the Hunt brothers could no longer meet calls on their borrowed position, and trading in the shares of their broker Bache was suspended. The S&P 500 ended March at 102.09, down 10% in the month.
why: The low point of the 1980 recession scare and the first big market month of the game. The Fed soon eased, and shares recovered all of it by the summer.

title: 1980 in review: shares up 26 percent despite record interest rates
what: The S&P 500 ended 1980 at 135.76, up 26% on the year, after falling to about 102 in March. The Dow Jones average closed the year at 963.99, up 14.9%. The year closes with the Federal Reserve's key interest rate approaching 20 percent as it fights inflation, and on 19 December the banks' prime rate reached a record 21.5 percent, a heavy weight on shares going into 1981.
why: A strong year that hid the danger ahead: Volcker's second squeeze of 1981 pushed the economy into a deep recession and shares into a 20-month bear market.

title: 1981 in review: high interest rates push shares down 10 percent
what: The S&P 500 fell 10% in 1981 to 122.55, and the Dow closed the year at 875.00, down 9.2%. The Dow had reached 1,024 in April on hopes for Reagan's tax cuts, but the Federal Reserve kept credit tight: its discount rate hit a record 14 percent in May, and the economy slid into recession in the second half. The Fed began to cut the discount rate in November, to 12 percent.
why: The middle of the 1980-82 bear market. Volcker's 'we mean to stick with it' policy broke inflation at the cost of the worst recession since the war.

title: 1982 in review: from the August low to records
what: The S&P 500 rose 15% in 1982 to 140.64, and the Dow gained 19.6% to 1,046.54, its best year in seven, after reaching an all-time high of 1,070.55 on 27 December. From the August low the Dow is up 37.7%. A record 16.46 billion shares traded on the New York Stock Exchange, while unemployment is near 11 percent, the highest since the war.
why: The year the bull market was born, in the middle of the worst recession since the 1930s.

title: 1983 in review: the recovery year, shares up 17 percent
what: The S&P 500 gained 17% in 1983 to 164.93; it first closed above 150 on 1 March. The Dow ended at 1,258.64, up 20.3%. Inflation, above 10 percent in 1981, is down to about 3 percent, and unemployment is falling from its peak of 10.8 percent a year ago.
why: A calm year of recovery between the 1982 turn and the 1984 pause.

title: A bond rally lifts shares 11 percent in August
what: Interest rates fell sharply over the summer, with yields on bonds down about 5/8 to 3/4 of a percentage point since mid-July, as the economy's expansion turned out slower than expected. Shares jumped with bonds: the S&P 500 rose 11% in August to 166.68. Earlier in the summer the Fed chairman, Paul Volcker, and the head of the SEC, John Shad, warned about the mountains of debt being piled up in takeovers.
why: One of the biggest months of the decade, driven by falling rates. The takeover warning is the first sign of the leveraged buyout boom that defines the late 1980s.

title: 1984 in review: a flat year as rates rise and fall
what: The S&P 500 ended 1984 at 167.24, up only 1%, and the Dow fell 3.7% to 1,211.57. Interest rates rose in the first half, with the prime rate peaking at 13 percent in June, then fell back to 10.75 percent by 19 December. Shares are roughly where they were at the end of 1983.
why: The pause in the bull market. Falling rates in the second half set up the strong years 1985 and 1986.

title: 1985 in review: shares up 26 percent in a year of takeovers
what: The S&P 500 rose 26% in 1985 to 211.28 and first closed above 200 on 21 November. The Dow ended at 1,546.67, up 27.7%, after 36 record closes. Falling interest rates and the September agreement of the five big economies at the Plaza Hotel to push the dollar down helped shares, and takeover bids financed with borrowed money, often with high-yield 'junk' bonds sold by Drexel Burnham Lambert, have made many shareholders rich.
why: The heart of the 1980s bull market and of the takeover boom; the debt behind it is what made 1987 and 1989 fragile.

title: Rising bond yields send shares down 9 percent
what: Shares fell sharply in September as long-term interest rates rose: yields on Treasury bonds climbed as much as 0.6 percentage point in a few weeks, although the Federal Reserve had cut its discount rate in August. Germany and Japan did not follow the American rate cut, raising worries about the dollar. The S&P 500 lost 9% in the month to 231.32, its worst month since March 1980.
why: A warning shot a year before the 1987 crash: the same mix of rising bond yields and dollar worries returned in October 1987.

title: 1986 in review: another strong year
what: The S&P 500 rose 15% in 1986 to 242.17, after first closing above 250 on 30 June; the Dow gained 22.6% to 1,895.95, after passing 1,750 in March. September showed how quickly shares can fall when bond yields rise.
why: The fourth year of the bull market; the speculative climax comes in 1987.

title: The Dow passes 2,000 as shares soar 13 percent in January
what: The Dow Jones average closed above 2,000 for the first time on 8 January, and shares kept climbing all month to new highs. The S&P 500 rose 13% in January to 274.08, its biggest monthly gain since at least 1975.
why: The start of the speculative run-up of 1987: by August the S&P 500 was up another 23%, and in October it all came down.

title: Shares hit a record as Greenspan takes over the Fed
what: The S&P 500 closed at a record 336.77 on 25 August and the Dow at 2,722.42, both up more than a third since New Year. Alan Greenspan was sworn in on 11 August as chairman of the Federal Reserve, taking over from Paul Volcker with the dollar weak and interest rates rising. Volcker leaves after eight years in which inflation fell from a peak of 14.8 percent in March 1980 to 3.9 percent (July), and the 10-year Treasury yield from 15.3 percent in September 1981 to 8.8 percent in August. The numbers: the Fed's rate 6.75 percent. Inflation 3.9 percent. Unemployment 6.1 percent.
why: The peak before the crash; the S&P 500 did not close above it again until July 1989.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closing_milestones_of_the_S%26P_500 (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closing_milestones_of_the_Dow_Jones_Industrial_Average (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Monday_(1987) (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Volcker (read 2026-10-04); https://fred.stlouisfed.org/data/CPIAUCNS.txt (read 2026-10-04); https://fred.stlouisfed.org/data/GS10.txt (read 2026-10-04); https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/FEDFUNDS, DFEDTAR, DFEDTARL, DFEDTARU, CPIAUCNS and UNRATE (downloaded 2026-10-04)
changed: interest-rate storyline: the numbers line now gives the Fed's target at the end of the month (not the monthly average) and the headline inflation figure, so it agrees with the text

title: Black Monday: the S&P 500 falls 20 percent in a day
what: After a bad trade deficit report on 14 October pushed interest rates up, shares fell 9% in a week; then on Monday 19 October the Dow plunged 508 points or 22.6% and the S&P 500 20.5%, the largest one-day falls in their history. Blamed are the dollar and the trade deficit, rising interest rates, a public row between Treasury Secretary Baker and Germany over the dollar, a bill to curb tax breaks for takeovers, and 'portfolio insurance' programs that sold automatically as prices fell. On 20 October the Fed said it stood ready to supply cash to the financial system; markets around the world crashed too, and the S&P 500 ended October down 22% at 251.79.
why: The defining crash of the game's early years. It is also the lesson that buying after a crash paid: the market was higher two years later.

title: No relief after the crash: the dollar slides and shares fall another 9 percent
what: Markets stayed unsettled after the October crash, with wide price swings and flights to safety. The dollar fell about 5% against the other big currencies, and the S&P 500 lost another 9% in November to 230.30, about 32% below its August record.
why: The real low of the 1987 bear market; from here the recovery began, slowly.

title: 1987 in review: up 2 percent, after the wildest year in memory
what: The S&P 500 ended 1987 at 247.08, up 2% on the year, after rising 39% to its August record and then losing a third of its value in two months. The Dow closed at 1,938.83, up 2.3%. So far the crash has had little visible effect on business activity, and interest rates are lower than before it.
why: The year's flat result hides the whole drama; a player who held on lost nothing over the year, one who sold in October locked in the loss.

title: Shares climb back above their pre-crash record
what: The S&P 500 rose 9% in July to 346.08, and on 26 July it closed above its August 1987 record of 336.77 for the first time since the crash. Interest rates have fallen since the spring, and the Dow closed above 2,600 on 21 July.
why: The full recovery from Black Monday, less than two years later.

title: Friday the 13th: a failed buyout knocks the Dow down 7 percent
what: On Friday 13 October the Dow fell 190.58 points or 6.9% and the S&P 500 6.1%, after financing for a 6.75 billion dollar buyout of UAL, the parent of United Airlines, fell apart. The indexes had closed at records only four days earlier. The failure raises doubts about the junk-bond market that pays for such deals.
why: The end of the takeover boom; the junk-bond market collapsed and Drexel went bankrupt in February 1990.

title: 1989 in review: up 27 percent and above the 1987 peak
what: The S&P 500 gained 27% in 1989 to 353.40, its best year since the bull market began, and the Dow rose 27.0% to 2,753.20. Both are now above their pre-crash records. The October scare raised doubts whether the takeover boom, which drove much of the rise, can keep finding borrowed money.
why: The last year of the 1980s boom before the 1990 recession. Review 2026-10: softened a hindsight verdict on the takeover boom.

title: Iraq's invasion of Kuwait sends shares down 9 percent
what: Iraq invaded Kuwait on 2 August; oil prices jumped and markets around the world fell. The rise in energy prices pushed long-term interest rates up, and share prices, which had set records in July, fell substantially. The S&P 500 lost 9% in August to 322.56. German shares were hit harder still: Daimler-Benz lost 16%. Kuwait's state investment office is one of its biggest shareholders, with about 14% held since 1974, and nobody knows what becomes of Kuwait's holdings abroad.
why: The market's reaction to the Gulf crisis (the cause is told in the Middle East and oil arcs). It tipped a weak economy into recession. The link between Daimler's fall and the Kuwaiti stake is the curator's point; the 16% is from the data, the worry about the holdings is stated as open, not sourced. [Curator note applied 2026-10-04: "Add a note that Kuwait is one of Daimler's biggest shareholders."]
source: https://www.upi.com/Archives/1990/08/02/Invasion-of-Kuwait-churns-international-markets/2008649569600 (read 2026-10-03); https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/files/fomcropa19900821.pdf (read 2026-10-03); data/reference/sp500.json; Kuwait's Daimler-Benz stake: Mercedes-Benz Classic chronicle as cited in the mercedes arc; price change from data/out/mercedes.json

title: 1990 in review: recession and the Gulf crisis cost 7 percent
what: The S&P 500 fell 7% in 1990 to 330.22; the Dow, down 18% from July to its low of 2,381.99 on 16 October, ended at 2,633.66, off 4.3%. Economists say the economy is in recession, and how deep it gets depends on war or peace in the Gulf. Banks are hurting from bad property loans: Citicorp, the biggest, plans to cut its dividend and 8,000 jobs, and the Fed cut its discount rate to 6.5 percent in December.
why: The only down year between 1981 and 1994. The October low was the bottom: the 1990s boom started from here.

title: The Fed cuts sharply and shares end 1991 with an 11 percent burst
what: On 20 December the Federal Reserve cut its interest rate to 4 percent, and the rate at which it lends to banks directly by a full point to 3.5 percent, the lowest in 27 years, to revive a sluggish economy. Shares soared: the Dow set four record closes in a row to end the year at 3,168.83, up 20.3% in 1991, and the S&P 500 rose 11% in December alone to 417.09, up 26% for the year. The recession never quite lifted this year, but falling interest rates lifted the markets. The numbers: the Fed's rate 4 percent. Inflation 3.0 percent. Unemployment 7.0 percent.
why: A year-end burst and the start of the 1990s bull market proper; the year's big gain came despite a weak economy.
source: https://www.upi.com/Archives/1991/12/20/Fed-slashes-discount-rate-to-35-percent/6075693205200/ (read 2026-10-03); https://archive.seattletimes.com/archive/19920102/1468134/the-market-in-1991----record-year-for-stocks----northwest-stocks-do-well-in-strange-year-end-rally (read 2026-10-03); https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/files/fomcropa19911217.pdf (read 2026-10-03); data/reference/sp500.json; https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/FEDFUNDS, DFEDTAR, DFEDTARL, DFEDTARU, CPIAUCNS and UNRATE (downloaded 2026-10-04)
changed: interest-rate storyline: the numbers line now gives the Fed's target at the end of the month (not the monthly average) and the headline inflation figure, so it agrees with the text; the text named only the discount rate, a different rate

title: 1993 in review: low interest rates, modest gains
what: The S&P 500 gained 7% in 1993 to 466.45. The Dow closed above 3,500 for the first time on 19 May and ended the year at 3,754.09, up 13.7%. The yield on 30-year Treasury bonds has fallen to about 6.2 percent, which helps shares and borrowers.
why: The calm before the 1994 bond shock.

title: 1994 in review: the Fed's rate rises bring the bond market's worst year
what: The S&P 500 fell 2% in 1994 to 459.27, while the Dow edged up 2.1%. Starting on 4 February the Federal Reserve raised its key rate from 3 to 5.5 percent by November, and the yield on 30-year Treasury bonds rose from 6.2 to 8.2 percent; bond investors lost about 1.5 trillion dollars worldwide. At year's end Mexico's markets are in crisis.
why: A losing year for shares and a terrible one for bonds, but the Fed's early move kept inflation down and set up the boom of 1995-99.

title: 1995 in review: shares up 34 percent, the best year in twenty years
what: The S&P 500 rose 34% in 1995 to 615.93, after first closing above 500 on 24 March. The Dow passed 4,000 on 23 February and 5,000 on 21 November and ended the year at 5,117.12, up 33.5%. The economy has absorbed the Fed's rate rises of 1994, and investment in new technology picked up late in the year.
why: The start of the great late-1990s boom: five years in a row of gains above 19%.
changed: note to the writer addressed: no reference to the game; our index data from 1975 shows no better year before 1995 (1980: +26 percent)

title: Greenspan asks about 'irrational exuberance'; shares end 1996 up 20 percent
what: On 5 December Fed chairman Alan Greenspan asked in a speech how one can know 'when irrational exuberance has unduly escalated asset values'. Tokyo, open at the time, fell 3% and markets around the world followed. Still, the S&P 500 ended 1996 up 20% at 740.74, and the Dow, which passed 6,000 on 14 October, up 26%.
why: The most famous warning of the 1990s, more than three years too early: the S&P 500 doubled again before the peak in 2000.

title: 1997 in review: up 31 percent, despite Asia
what: The S&P 500 gained 31% in 1997 to 970.43; it passed 800 on 12 February, and the Dow ended at 7,908.24, up 22.6%. The October scare from Asia was quickly made good.
why: The third year in a row above 20%.

title: A surprise Fed cut on 15 October and shares bounce 8 percent
what: Shares fell further in early October, then on 15 October the Federal Reserve cut its key rate again, to about 5 percent, without waiting for a meeting. The market rallied strongly after mid-October as fears of a financial breakdown eased. The S&P 500 rose 8% in October to 1,098.67. The numbers: the Fed's rate 5 percent. Inflation 1.5 percent. Unemployment 4.6 percent.
why: The Fed's three cuts in autumn 1998 ended the panic and fuelled the final, wildest phase of the dot-com boom.
source: https://www.federalreserve.gov/fomc/minutes/19981117.htm (read 2026-10-03); data/reference/sp500.json; https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/FEDFUNDS, DFEDTAR, DFEDTARL, DFEDTARU, CPIAUCNS and UNRATE (downloaded 2026-10-04)
changed: interest-rate storyline: the numbers line now gives the Fed's target at the end of the month (not the monthly average) and the headline inflation figure, so it agrees with the text

title: 1998 in review: a panic in the middle, up 27 percent in the end
what: The S&P 500 rose 27% in 1998 to 1,229.23, after first closing above 1,000 on 2 February and falling 15% in August alone. The Dow passed 9,000 on 6 April and ended at 9,181.43, up 16.1%. The Fed's autumn rate cuts brought the buyers back.
why: The fourth year in a row above 20%; the summer showed how fast it could turn.

title: Dow 10,000
what: The Dow Jones average closed above 10,000 for the first time on 29 March, celebrated on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange with party hats. It was below 4,000 at the start of 1995.
why: The symbol of the 1990s boom; the Dow did not stay convincingly above 10,000 until 2003.

title: The Nasdaq tops 5,000 and the S&P 500 sets a record
what: The Nasdaq index closed at a record 5,048.62 on 10 March, and the S&P 500 rose 10% in March, closing above 1,500 for the first time on 22 March and setting a new record on 24 March. Fed officials worry that the high valuations of many technology shares could see a sizable correction, as the market grows more volatile.
why: The top of the dot-com bubble. The S&P 500 did not close above this level for seven years, the Nasdaq for fifteen. Review 2026-10: 'peaks' was hindsight.

title: 2000 in review: the first losing year in a decade
what: The S&P 500 fell 10% in 2000 to 1,320.28, its first losing year since 1994 and its worst since 1977; the Dow lost 6.2%. Internet shares have collapsed: most are down 75% or more from their highs, and the dot-com crash has wiped out about 1.75 trillion dollars of value by November.
why: Year one of the 2000-02 bear market.

title: A surprise rate cut and better earnings bring an 8 percent bounce
what: On 18 April the Federal Reserve cut its key rate by half a point to 4.5 percent between meetings, its fourth cut this year. Together with better-than-expected first-quarter earnings, the surprise lifted shares substantially: the S&P 500 rose 8% in April to 1,249.46. The numbers: the Fed's rate 4.5 percent. Inflation 2.9 percent. Unemployment 4.3 percent.
why: A bear-market rally; the low was still eighteen months away.
source: https://www.federalreserve.gov/fomc/minutes/20010515.htm (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Federal_Open_Market_Committee_actions (read 2026-10-03); data/reference/sp500.json; https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/FEDFUNDS, DFEDTAR, DFEDTARL, DFEDTARU, CPIAUCNS and UNRATE (downloaded 2026-10-04)
changed: interest-rate storyline: the numbers line now gives the Fed's target at the end of the month (not the monthly average) and the headline inflation figure, so it agrees with the text

title: Good news from Afghanistan and the economy lifts shares 8 percent
what: Shares rose significantly in November on better-than-expected economic data and favourable news on the military campaign in Afghanistan. The Fed cut its key rate again on 6 November, to 2 percent. The S&P 500 gained 8% in the month to 1,139.45, above where it stood before 11 September.
why: The post-9/11 recovery; it fizzled in 2002 as accounting scandals spread.

title: 2001 in review: eleven rate cuts cannot stop a second losing year
what: The S&P 500 fell 13% in 2001 to 1,148.08 and the Dow 7.1%, a second losing year in a row. The Federal Reserve cut its key rate eleven times during the year, from 6.5 to 1.75 percent, as the economy fell into recession and the September attacks shook confidence.
why: Year two of the bust; the worst, the accounting scandals of 2002, was still to come.

title: WorldCom's collapse caps a month of accounting scandals
what: WorldCom, brought down by an accounting scandal, filed for bankruptcy on 21 July, the largest corporate insolvency ever. Revelations of corporate fraud and fears of more restated earnings sent shares plunging; President Bush gave a stern speech on accounting scandals on 9 July, and the Dow closed below 8,000 on 23 July before a late rebound. The S&P 500 lost 8% in July to 911.62. The head of the FCC told the Senate that the telecom industry owes about a trillion dollars, much of which will never be repaid, and the Nasdaq fell 9% in July to 1,328.
why: The crisis of trust that turned the bust into a three-year bear market.

title: Iraq tensions and weak data: shares fall 11 percent
what: Weak figures on production and jobs, a gloomier outlook for profits and rising tension over Iraq sent shares down again in September. On 23 September the Nasdaq hit a six-year low and the yield on 10-year Treasury bonds sank to 3.70 percent, a 40-year low, as investors fled to safety. The S&P 500 lost 11% in the month to 815.28. The Nasdaq ended the month at 1,172, 77% below its record of March 2000, as accounting scandals from Enron to WorldCom shook trust in company figures.
why: The final leg down of the 2000-02 bear market.

title: 2002 in review: a third losing year in a row
what: The S&P 500 fell 23% in 2002 to 879.82, its third losing year in a row and its worst of the game so far; it is 40% below where it stood at the end of 1999. The Dow lost 16.8% to 8,341.63. Accounting scandals, the WorldCom and Enron bankruptcies, a weak economy and the threat of war with Iraq weighed on shares, and the Fed cut its key rate to 1.25 percent in November.
why: The end of the bust. A player who bought here doubled their money by 2007.

title: 2003 in review: the bull returns, up 26 percent
what: The S&P 500 rose 26% in 2003 to 1,111.92, its first gain in four years, and the Dow 25.3% to 10,453.92. The Federal Reserve cut its key rate to 1 percent in June, and the end of major fighting in Iraq and rising profits brought investors back.
why: Cheap money lifted shares and, less visibly, house prices: the seed of 2008.

title: 2004 in review: steady gains as the Fed starts raising rates
what: The S&P 500 gained 9% in 2004 to 1,211.92 and the Dow 3.2%. The Federal Reserve began raising its key rate on 30 June, in quarter-point steps from 1 to 2.25 percent by December, as the recovery gathered strength.
why: A quiet middle year of the 2003-07 bull market.

title: Flipping houses: how ordinary Americans get rich on borrowed money
what: In America a new way to get rich is called 'flipping': buy a house with borrowed money, wait a few months, sell it for more, and buy two. A 22-year-old from Las Vegas tells the magazine Fortune that he bought 15 houses in Phoenix with 150,000 dollars of his own money; seven months later they are worth 3 million instead of 2 million. A couple who started with five houses and 1,000 dollars down on each now own twenty. It works because house prices only seem to rise, by 77 percent in New York, 92 percent in Miami and 105 percent in San Diego since 2000, and because banks ask for very little: almost a third of all new mortgages last year were loans on which the borrower pays only the interest and nothing back, against fewer than two in a hundred in 2001. Nearly a quarter of all homes are now bought by investors, not by people who want to live in them.
why: The build-up to the crisis in one story: cheap loans, rising prices, and people who believe that houses cannot fall. The television show 'Flip This House' started that July; in 2005 investors bought 28 percent of all homes sold. Prices began to fall in 2006.
source: https://fortune.com/2013/07/14/riding-the-boom-fortune-2005 (Fortune, 2005, republished; read 2026-10-04); https://www.nar.realtor/blogs/economists-outlook/share-of-homes-sold-by-use-2001-to-2010 (search result read 2026-10-04); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flip_This_House (search result read 2026-10-04)

title: Home prices up 15 percent in a year; Greenspan sees 'froth'
what: Americans bought existing homes at a record annual rate of 7.33 million in June, and the median price reached a record 219,000 dollars, 14.7 percent more than a year earlier, the biggest jump since 1980. On 9 June Fed chairman Alan Greenspan told Congress that exceptionally low interest rates on home mortgages were a major factor in the steep climb in home prices, and that there were 'at a minimum, signs of froth in some local markets'. He called the rapid spread of interest-only loans and other exotic adjustable-rate mortgages a particular concern. A 30-year mortgage costs about 5.7 percent.
why: The housing boom at full speed: the Fed had been raising its rate for a year, but mortgage rates barely moved, so cheap money kept flowing into homes. Between 2004 and 2006 subprime loans made up 18 to 21 percent of all new mortgages.

title: 2005 in review: a flat year under rising rates
what: The S&P 500 rose only 3% in 2005 to 1,248.29, and the Dow slipped 0.6%. The Federal Reserve raised its key rate at every meeting of the year, eight times, to 4.25 percent.
why: Shares marked time while housing boomed.

title: House prices are falling
what: The median price of an existing single-family home fell to 219,800 dollars in September, 2.5 percent less than a year earlier and the biggest drop in records going back nearly four decades; prices had also fallen in August. Sales slowed to an annual rate of 6.18 million, the lowest since January 2004, and 3.75 million unsold homes are on the market, enough for 7.3 months. Between June 2004 and June 2006 the Fed raised its rate seventeen times, from 1 to 5.25 percent, and the era of cheap mortgages is over. The realtors' chief economist says 'the worst is behind us'.
why: The first clear crack: national house prices falling year on year, which every loan written on the assumption of rising prices could not survive. The optimism was misplaced; prices kept falling and reached new lows only in 2011.

title: 2006 in review: the Dow at a record, for the first time since 2000
what: The S&P 500 rose 14% in 2006 to 1,418.30, and the Dow gained 16.3% to 12,463.15 after closing above 12,000 for the first time on 19 October, beating its record of January 2000. The Federal Reserve stopped raising rates in June, at 5.25 percent.
why: The bull market in full swing, a year before the credit crisis began.

title: Subprime lender New Century stops lending
what: New Century Financial, the biggest independent lender to home buyers with weak credit, so-called subprime borrowers, said on 8 March that it would stop accepting loan applications. Its shares lost 89 percent in March before the New York Stock Exchange halted trading on the 12th and removed them a day later. Last year New Century made 51.6 billion dollars of subprime loans, more than any lender except HSBC Finance.
why: The first big casualty of the housing bust: with prices no longer rising, weak borrowers defaulted and lenders that lived on selling loans to Wall Street could no longer fund themselves. New Century filed for bankruptcy on 2 April, and about 3,200 people lost their jobs.

title: Two Bear Stearns funds lose nearly everything on subprime bets
what: In the week of 16 July the Wall Street investment bank Bear Stearns disclosed that two of its hedge funds, invested in securities built from subprime mortgages, had lost nearly all their value. In June Bear Stearns had pledged loans of up to 3.2 billion dollars to rescue one of them. The S&P 500 fell 3 percent in July.
why: The housing losses reach Wall Street: the first sign that banks and their funds held the bad mortgages themselves. Bear Stearns itself collapsed eight months later.

title: Credit markets freeze: BNP Paribas blocks funds, the Fed steps in
what: On 9 August the French bank BNP Paribas blocked withdrawals from three funds invested in American mortgage securities, citing 'a complete evaporation of liquidity'. Banks stopped trusting each other, and on 17 August the Federal Reserve cut its discount rate by half a point to 5.75 percent and offered banks loans of up to 30 days against mortgages and other collateral. Shares swung wildly but the S&P 500 ended August up 1%.
why: The start of the financial crisis, a year before Lehman. The market did not yet believe it. Review 2026-10: 'begins' presumed the later crisis.

title: The S&P 500 sets a record after Fed rate cuts
what: After the Federal Reserve cut its key rate by half a point to 4.75 percent in September, shares rallied, and the S&P 500 closed at a record 1,565.15 on 9 October, just above its 2000 peak. The Dow reached about 14,164. The Fed cut again on 31 October, to 4.5 percent.
why: The top of the 2003-07 bull market; seventeen months later the index had lost 57%.

title: 2007 in review: up 4 percent, with the credit crisis spreading
what: The S&P 500 ended 2007 up 4% at 1,468.36 and the Dow up 6.4%, after the October record. The credit crisis that began in August is not over, and the Federal Reserve has cut its key rate three times since September, to 4.25 percent.
why: The last up year before the crash. The recession later dated as starting in December 2007 was not yet known.

title: The Fed's emergency cut: three-quarters of a point between meetings
what: As shares fell around the world, the Federal Reserve cut its key rate by 0.75 percentage point to 3.5 percent on 22 January without waiting for its meeting, its largest cut in 25 years, and by another half point on 30 January. The S&P 500 still lost 6% in January to 1,378.55. The numbers: the Fed's rate 3 percent. Inflation 4.1 percent. Unemployment 5.0 percent.
why: The Fed fighting the crisis early; markets read it as a sign of how bad things were.

changed: interest-rate storyline: the numbers line now gives the Fed's target at the end of the month (not the monthly average) and the headline inflation figure, so it agrees with the text

title: Bear Stearns is rescued by JPMorgan for 2 dollars a share
what: The investment bank Bear Stearns, heavy with 46 billion dollars of mortgage assets, faced collapse in mid-March. On 16-17 March JPMorgan Chase agreed to buy it for 2 dollars a share, with the Fed guaranteeing bad loans; the shares were at 60 dollars a week earlier and 178 a year ago. The Fed cut its key rate by another 0.75 point to 2.25 percent on 18 March.
why: The first big Wall Street casualty. Because Bear was saved, many assumed Lehman would be too.

title: Record oil and bank losses send shares down 9 percent
what: Oil jumped nearly 11 dollars on 6 June to a record 138.54 dollars a barrel, raising fears of inflation and recession at once. Banks kept reporting mortgage losses: Wachovia, the fourth-largest American bank, ousted its chief executive on 2 June, and General Motors announced plant closures and 10,000 job cuts. The S&P 500 lost 9% in June to 1,280.00.
why: The squeeze between oil (told in the oil arc) and the banks; the worst was three months away.

title: The House votes down the bailout and the Dow falls 778 points
what: On 7 September the government took over the two big mortgage companies Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, which had more than 5 trillion dollars of mortgage securities and debt outstanding. On 20 September Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson asked Congress for 700 billion dollars to buy toxic mortgage assets ('If it doesn't pass, then heaven help us all'). On 29 September the House of Representatives rejected the bill 225 to 208; the Dow fell 777.68 points, its largest point drop ever, and the S&P 500 8.8%. The S&P 500 ended September down 9% at 1,166.36. Mining shares were hit hard as credit froze: copper averaged $6,991 a tonne in September, 17% below July, and Xstrata lost 45% in the month.
why: Politics meets panic; the vote was reversed days later, but October was worse.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_financial_crisis (read 2026-10-03); data/reference/sp500.json; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_takeover_of_Fannie_Mae_and_Freddie_Mac (read 2026-10-04); Xstrata circular 2 Feb 2009 (current trading and prospects), https://www.rns-pdf.londonstockexchange.com/rns/6630M_-2009-2-2.pdf; World Bank Pink Sheet monthly averages (both read 2026-10-03)

title: Crash month: the worst week ever, then the biggest daily gain since the 1930s
what: Congress passed the 700 billion dollar rescue on 3 October, but panic spread worldwide: in the week of 6 to 10 October the Dow fell 18.2%, its worst week ever, and on 8 October central banks cut rates together in an emergency move. On 13 October the S&P 500 jumped 11.6%, then fell 9.0% on 15 October and rose 10.8% on 28 October. The S&P 500 lost 17% in October to 968.75, its worst month since the 1987 crash.
why: The climax of the panic; the biggest monthly fall of the game after October 1987.

title: 2008 in review: shares lose 38 percent
what: The S&P 500 fell 38% in 2008 to 903.25, its worst year in the game's data, and the Dow 33.8% to 8,776.39. On 1 December economists declared that a recession had begun in December 2007, and the S&P 500 fell 8.9% that day. On 16 December the Federal Reserve cut its key rate to between 0 and 0.25 percent, as low as it can go.
why: The worst year of the game. The final low came in March 2009, 57% below the 2007 peak.

title: Bank losses and a new rescue: the worst January for shares
what: Big banks reported large losses from trading, write-downs and bad loans, and on 16 January the government agreed to give Bank of America guarantees, cash and capital after its takeover of Merrill Lynch. Bank shares fell below their November lows, and the S&P 500 lost 9% in January to 825.88.
why: The second wave of the crisis: fear that the big banks would have to be nationalized.

title: Doubts about the bank rescue push shares to 12-year lows
what: Congress approved a 787 billion dollar stimulus package on 13 February, but investors were uneasy about the Treasury's new plan to stabilize the banks and about what the government might do next. Bank and insurance shares were hit hardest; on 27 February the government agreed to take a 36% stake in Citigroup, and the Dow closed at its lowest level since 1997. The S&P 500 lost 11% in February to 735.09.
why: The capitulation before the bottom.

title: The S&P 500 sinks to 676, then a sudden rally
what: The S&P 500 closed at 676.53 on 9 March, 57% below its October 2007 record, and the Dow at 6,547.05, its lowest since 1997. On 10 March Citigroup said it had been profitable in January and February, and its shares jumped 38% while the indexes rose 5 to 7%. On 18 March the Fed said it would buy up to 300 billion dollars of Treasury bonds and 750 billion more of mortgage securities. The S&P 500 ended March up 9% at 797.87.
why: The bottom of the 2007-09 bear market and the start of a bull market that lasted eleven years, until February 2020. Few believed it at the time. Review 2026-10: 'The bottom' was hindsight.

title: Banks report profits and the rally runs on
what: Shares rose strongly again in April, helped by the government's measures to clean up bank balance sheets and by favourable first-quarter earnings from a few big banks; financial shares led. On 10 April Time magazine wrote that the banking crisis was ending 'more quickly than it began'. Investors are nervous about the results of the government's stress tests of the big banks, due in May. The S&P 500 rose 9% in April to 872.81.
why: The early bull market climbing a wall of worry.

title: 2009 in review: up 23 percent, and 65 percent from the March low
what: The S&P 500 rose 23% in 2009 to 1,115.10, 65% above its March low, and the Dow 18.8%. The Federal Reserve kept its key rate near zero all year and bought bonds on a huge scale, but unemployment has risen to about 10 percent.
why: A year of recovery that rewarded those who held on through the March panic.

title: America loses its AAA rating and shares plunge
what: Late on 5 August Standard and Poor's cut the United States' credit rating from AAA to AA+, the first time the country has lost the agency's top rating, after a bitter fight in Congress over the debt ceiling. On Monday 8 August the S&P 500 fell 6.7% to 1,119.46, as fears grew that Europe's debt crisis would spread to Italy and Spain and that America would fall back into recession. European regulators banned short selling of bank shares from 11 August, and the S&P 500 ended August down 6%. Investors fled into Treasury bonds and gold, which averaged a record 1,759 dollars in August, 12 percent more than in July. In Germany the DAX fell from 7,376 at the end of June to around 5,250 in early September, with car makers hit hardest; Daimler's shares lost 26% in August.
why: The euro crisis summer; the cause is told in the Europe arc. The S&P 500 fell about 20% from May to early October.

title: 2011 in review: a year of turmoil ends exactly flat
what: The S&P 500 ended 2011 at 1,257.60, almost exactly where it began (1,257.64), after falling about 21% between May and October. The Dow gained 5.5%. America's downgrade and Europe's debt crisis made it one of the most volatile years in memory.
why: A lesson in noise: all that drama for a zero.

title: 2012 in review: up 13 percent, with the fiscal cliff looming
what: The S&P 500 rose 13% in 2012 to 1,426.19 and the Dow 7.3%. As the year ends, Congress has not yet agreed how to avoid the 'fiscal cliff': tax rises and spending cuts that take effect on 1 January and that the Congressional Budget Office says would likely cause a mild recession.
why: A good year despite politics; the cliff was averted on 1 January 2013.

title: 2013 in review: up 30 percent, the best year since 1997
what: The S&P 500 gained 30% in 2013 to 1,848.36, its best year since 1997, and the Dow 26.5%. The Dow set its first record since 2007 on 5 March and passed 16,000 on 21 November, while the Federal Reserve kept interest rates near zero and bought bonds every month.
why: The year the bull market finally erased the 2008 crash.

title: 2014 in review: the S&P 500 passes 2,000
what: The S&P 500 rose 11% in 2014 to 2,058.90, after first closing above 2,000 on 26 August; the Dow gained 7.5%. The Federal Reserve ended its bond-buying programme in October.
why: A steady year in a long bull market.

title: Shares win back the summer's losses in October
what: After falling in late September, shares more than recovered as worries about world growth eased, foreign central banks were expected to ease policy and figures from China were better than feared. The S&P 500 rose 8% in October to 2,079.36.
why: The rebound after the China scare; another dip followed in January 2016.

title: 2015 in review: a flat year and the first Fed rate rise since 2006
what: The S&P 500 slipped 1% in 2015 to 2,043.94 and the Dow 2.2%, after the August scare over China and a slump in oil. On 16 December the Federal Reserve raised its key rate for the first time since June 2006, to between 0.25 and 0.5 percent.
why: The end of the zero-rate era; a pause in the bull market.

title: 2016 in review: Brexit, Trump and a 10 percent gain
what: The S&P 500 rose 10% in 2016 to 2,238.83 and the Dow 13.4%. Britain's vote to leave the European Union on 23 June wiped about 2 trillion dollars off world markets the next day, but American shares were at records by July. After Donald Trump won the presidential election in November shares rallied, and the Dow passed 19,000 on 22 November; the Fed raised rates for the second time on 14 December.
why: Two political shocks the market shrugged off.

title: 2017 in review: a calm climb and a big tax cut
what: The S&P 500 gained 19% in 2017 to 2,673.61 and the Dow 25.1%, after passing 20,000 on 25 January. On 22 December President Trump signed a tax law that cuts the corporate tax rate to a flat 21%. The Federal Reserve raised rates three times during the year.
why: An unusually calm year; the calm ended abruptly in February 2018.

title: Volatility returns: the Dow falls 1,175 points in a day
what: A bigger-than-expected rise in wages in the January jobs report raised fears of inflation and faster rate rises. On 5 February the Dow fell 1,175 points or 4.6%, its largest point drop ever, and the VIX volatility index jumped to its highest since 2015 as bets on calm markets unwound; on 8 February the Dow fell another 1,033 points. The S&P 500 lost 4% in February.
why: The end of the 2017 calm; a preview of the fall at year's end. Review 2026-10: 'then' implied a later, bigger drop.

title: The Christmas fall: shares lose 9 percent in December
what: Worries about the trade war with China and slowing world growth, a Fed rate rise on 19 December that investors felt ignored the tightening in markets, and a partial government shutdown sent shares down hard. By Christmas Eve the S&P 500 stood at 2,351, nearly 20% below its September record, before the Dow jumped 1,086 points on 26 December. The S&P 500 lost 9% in December to 2,506.85 and 6% in 2018, its worst year since 2008; the Dow fell 5.6%. It was the Fed's fourth rise of the year, to 2.25 to 2.5 percent, and December was the S&P 500's worst month since February 2009. Government bonds, where investors seek safety when shares fall, rose: the US Treasury 2030 gained almost 4 percent. The numbers: the Fed's rate 2.25 to 2.5 percent. Inflation 2.2 percent. Unemployment 3.8 percent.
why: The near-bear market of 2018, which reversed as soon as the Fed changed its tone in January.

title: The Fed promises patience and shares jump 8 percent
what: Early in January Federal Reserve officials said the central bank could be 'patient' about further rate rises, and positive signals on trade with China followed. The S&P 500 rose 8% in January to 2,704.10, winning back most of December's loss. The numbers: the Fed's rate 2.25 to 2.5 percent. Inflation 1.9 percent. Unemployment 3.9 percent.
why: The Fed's U-turn; it cut rates three times later in 2019.

title: 2019 in review: up 29 percent as the Fed cuts rates
what: The S&P 500 gained 29% in 2019 to 3,230.78, after first closing above 3,000 on 12 July, and the Dow 22.3%. The Federal Reserve cut its key rate three times, in July, September and October, to between 1.5 and 1.75 percent.
why: A big year that set records just before the pandemic.

title: The coronavirus reaches the markets: the fastest fall from a record
what: The S&P 500 closed at a record 3,386.15 on 19 February. Then the new coronavirus spread beyond China, and in the week of 24 to 28 February markets had their largest weekly falls since the 2008 crisis, the fastest slide from a record ever seen. The S&P 500 ended February down 8% at 2,954.22. The virus reached northern Italy, where towns were sealed off, and Switzerland, which confirmed its first case on 25 February and on 28 February banned events with more than 1,000 people. Oil fell with shares: US crude closed February at about 45 dollars, from 61 at the end of December, and ExxonMobil lost 17%.
why: The start of the 2020 crash; the virus itself is told in the world arc.

title: The best month since 1987, in the middle of a pandemic
what: With the Fed's emergency lending programmes and the 2 trillion dollar CARES Act behind them, shares more than won back their late-March losses, led by energy, consumer and health-care companies. The S&P 500 rose 13% in April to 2,912.43, its best month since January 1987, though still well below February's record and with unemployment soaring.
why: The start of the fastest recovery ever: a record by August.

title: Back at a record, five months after the crash
what: On 18 August the S&P 500 closed above its February record, less than five months after the March low. The S&P 500 rose 7% in August to 3,500.31, while the pandemic still kept much of the economy closed.
why: The fastest recovery from a bear market ever, a lesson in not selling at the bottom.

title: 2020 in review: crash and recovery, up 16 percent
what: The S&P 500 ended 2020 at 3,756.07, up 16%, after falling 34% between February and March; the Dow gained 7.3%. Interest rates near zero, huge government spending and the vaccines carried shares to records despite the pandemic.
why: The year that showed how fast markets can fall and recover.

title: The GameStop frenzy: small investors squeeze the hedge funds
what: Users of the Reddit forum r/wallstreetbets piled into GameStop, a struggling video game retailer, whose shares had been heavily sold short by hedge funds; the stock rose from 17 dollars at New Year to as much as 483 dollars on 28 January. The hedge fund Melvin Capital needed a 2.75 billion dollar rescue, and on 28 January Robinhood and other brokers stopped customers from buying the shares, causing an outcry. Trading volumes beat the peaks of 2008, and the market had its worst week since October.
why: The mania of the zero-rate era and of trading apps; a lesson in bubbles.

title: 2021 in review: up 27 percent on cheap money
what: The S&P 500 rose 27% in 2021 to 4,766.18, after first closing above 4,000 on 1 April, and the Dow 18.7%, passing 36,000 on 2 November. Inflation rose fast during the year, but the Federal Reserve called it 'transitory' and kept its rate near zero.
why: The top of the cheap-money boom; the 2022 bear market started three days into the new year.

title: Rising rates and weak earnings: the worst month since March 2020
what: Long-term interest rates rose sharply as the Federal Reserve prepared bigger rate rises against inflation, some big companies reported disappointing earnings at the end of the month, and lockdowns in China clouded the world economy. The S&P 500 lost 9% in April to 4,131.93, its worst month since March 2020. The numbers: the Fed's rate 0.25 to 0.5 percent. Inflation 8.5 percent. Unemployment 3.7 percent.
why: The 2022 bear market gathering pace; technology shares were hit hardest (told in the tech arc).

title: A summer rally on falling yields: shares up 9 percent
what: Bond yields fell on fears of recession, and some better-than-feared earnings made investors less gloomy about companies' prospects. The S&P 500 rose 9% in July to 4,130.29, its best month since November 2020.
why: A bear-market rally; it ended at Jackson Hole in late August.

title: A new low for the year, then an 8 percent rebound
what: Shares fell further early in October on inflation news and rate expectations, with the S&P 500 closing at 3,577.03 on 12 October, about 25% below its January record. Then they rebounded, and the index ended October up 8% at 3,871.98.
why: The bottom of the 2022 bear market, the start of the AI-led bull market. Review 2026-10: 'The 2022 low' was hindsight.

title: 2022 in review: the worst year since 2008
what: The S&P 500 fell 19% in 2022 to 3,839.50, its worst year since 2008, and the Nasdaq 33%; the Dow lost 8.8%. The Federal Reserve raised its key rate seven times, from near zero to 4.25-4.5 percent, to fight inflation, and bonds fell as well as shares.
why: The year cheap money ended; one of the rare years when bonds offered no shelter.

title: Inflation cools, yields drop, shares jump 9 percent
what: Softer-than-expected inflation and other data convinced investors that the Federal Reserve had probably finished raising rates, and Treasury yields fell sharply from their October highs. The S&P 500 rose 9% in November to 4,567.80. The numbers: the Fed's rate 5.25 to 5.5 percent. Inflation 3.2 percent. Unemployment 3.9 percent.
why: The 'peak rates' rally that carried shares to records in early 2024.

title: 2023 in review: up 24 percent, out of the bear market
what: The S&P 500 gained 24% in 2023 to 4,769.83, just short of its January 2022 record, and the Dow 13.7%, passing 37,000 on 13 December. The index left its bear market on 8 June, 20% above the October 2022 low, despite the spring banking scare and rates raised to 5.25-5.5 percent in July.
why: The recovery year, led by a few giant technology companies (told in the tech arc).

title: A yen shock and weak jobs data: a one-day global scare
what: Weaker-than-expected American jobs figures and the unwinding of trades financed with cheap yen set off a global sell-off on Monday 5 August: Tokyo's Nikkei fell 12.4%, its worst day since 1987, and the Dow fell 1,034 points. The panic passed within days, and the S&P 500 ended August up 2%.
why: A scare that came from Japan (told in the Asia arc); the quick recovery is the point.

title: 2024 in review: up 23 percent, past 5,000 and 6,000
what: The S&P 500 rose 23% in 2024 to 5,881.63, after first closing above 5,000 on 9 February and above 6,000 on 11 November; the Dow gained 12.9%. The Federal Reserve began cutting rates in September, and after the November election the Dow jumped 1,508 points on 6 November.
why: The second strong year of the AI boom.

title: 2025 in review: a third double-digit year in a row
what: The S&P 500 gained 16% in 2025 to 6,845.50, the Nasdaq 19% and the Dow 13%, a third year in a row of double-digit gains. The April tariff crash became an afterthought, and resilient earnings, three Federal Reserve rate cuts from September and enthusiasm for artificial intelligence carried shares to records despite a long government shutdown and worries about an AI bubble.
why: The AI boom's third year; a rare streak that raised the stakes for 2026.

title: Ceasefire and strong earnings: the best month since 2020
what: President Trump announced a two-week ceasefire with Iran late on 7 April; the next day oil fell about 15% and the Dow jumped 1,326 points. The S&P 500 closed at a record 7,022.95 on 15 April, though the Strait of Hormuz stayed effectively closed, as 84% of companies beat profit forecasts and technology shares led on optimism about AI. The S&P 500 rose 10% in April to a record 7,209.01, its best month since November 2020.
why: A war-time rally to records; shares looked past the oil shock to earnings and AI.
